On Gmail spam filtering: one user found it frustrating that Google already seems to block mail from relatively new domains, yet obvious spam messages still get through.

A user who had just been complaining about the Gmail web app's interface hoped a real Gmail API would let developers build better interfaces on top, to improve inbox management and cut time spent sifting through email.

Gmail doesn't implement IMAP properly: IDLE only signals new messages, not changes in unread count. After moving from self-hosted Dovecot, the user was shocked that read status didn't propagate across devices until a manual poll.

A developer spent a year trying to replicate Gmail's interface in a desktop app (BetterInbox) over IMAP and said IMAP is completely unsuited to the Gmail paradigm. The new API would have made their lives much easier.

One developer's IMAP client code for Google Apps Gmail was 'full of hacks to convert internal ids to Gmail ids and format conversion issues'. They welcomed replacing it with a couple of HTTP calls via the Gmail API.
A user is very reluctant to give any third party access to their Gmail mailbox, because most sites allow password reset by email, so it's like handing over the keys to the castle.
Gmail API auth scopes already allow read-only access, but one user wants to restrict apps to a specific label or subfolder for better security without forwarding mail.
SMS Backup+ to Gmail has been 'fantastic for archiving all of my texts'. Each message is stored with the contact as sender, and the user can search everything relatively easily.
Workaround for Google's OAuth restrictions: GSuite admins can whitelist existing apps. The user did this for SMS Backup+ so it keeps working, but noted consumer Gmail users probably lack that option.
Facing Google's restrictions on third-party apps, one user stopped backing up to Google and instead synced SMS Backup to a local Dovecot IMAP server. Setup turned out to be incredibly simple.
A user said Google restricting seamless third-party integrations hurts utility and was 'just another reason I'm happy with moving my primary mail to FastMail on my own domain.'
Google lets anyone register my gmail address as their 'alternative recovery email' without confirmation, so I periodically get a dozen 'recover your account' emails from strangers' accounts.

A user with a fairly generic gmail address has hundreds of accounts linked to it that they never signed up for, because people mistype or don't know their own address. The account became unusable, so they switched to their own domain about a decade ago.

Gmail seems quite bad at filtering obvious spam: one user gets many messages from unknown senders on new domains, ending with lines like 'if this isn't relevant for you right now, say "not now"'. They are considering services that make senders confirm they're human.
Gmail's 'Tab to improve' prompt infuriates one user. They have their own voice and deliberately use 'bad' writing tropes for effect, so the feature amounts to 'tab to delete my own personality'.

An elderly mother read a Gmail AI summary of a supermarket delivery email, and it hallucinated the wrong delivery date. The only important information was the date. She was distressed, thinking her mental decline had accelerated. Her child disabled the AI features.

At work on Google Workspace, the AI features appeared in Gmail, Docs and Sheets, but the team turned them off without difficulty and hasn't been bothered since. It was just one more default setting to change.

One user accepts about 50% of Gmail's suggested improvements. They catch correctly spelled but unintended words using context, and sometimes make sentences clearer. But some turn a warm email into a cold business one, and those get ignored.
Google pushes Gemini aggressively, adding 'Write with AI' buttons everywhere. To use some AI features, you must opt in to Smart Features across all of Google Workspace, which the user doesn't want.

One user left Gmail when Google reneged on free custom-domain inboxes for grandfathered users and moved to iCloud+ for €0.99/month, which includes 50GB of storage and Hide My Email. No regrets so far.
One user often thinks about leaving Gmail, but it isn't clear what better option exists without the pain of losing replacements for the rest of the Google ecosystem.

Streak has used the Gmail API to build email snoozing and finds it really nice to use, making interaction with Gmail much easier than IMAP. However, listing threads doesn't return their messages, which makes building a full client hard.

Gmail API scopes only allow full control, read everything, everything except delete, or drafts. Granting that coarse access to third-party apps with no fine-grained control seems insane to one commenter.
One user finds Gmail's added widgets, such as RSVP on invitations and itineraries on flight booking emails, pretty useful.

A developer failed to publish a Gmail add-on because of the API lockdown. Apps needing read access must pass a third-party security assessment costing $75,000 USD per year, which shuts out small developers.
Gmail's own data export tools don't work at all for inboxes of considerable size (100GB+), so third-party tools are the only way to back up or migrate the data.

Because Gmail ignores dots, a user is getting another person's commercial HVAC account, library appointments and a lake-house down payment receipt. They wish Gmail could bounce mail that doesn't match their dot pattern.
Workaround: Gmail lets you filter in a dot-sensitive way. Mail missing one user's dot goes to a 'wrongguy' folder, which is mostly full of spam.
Gmail said 'try again later' every day for three weeks, even from the user's usual IP address. After 2–3 months it suddenly let them in. They'll never again use Gmail for critically important things.

Workarounds for lockout reported by users: digging out an old phone still signed into the account, connecting via VPN to the previous country of residence (after 4 months of trying), and an incognito tab.
Users with 2FA via Google Authenticator and emergency backup codes stored safely say they always get back in, with fewer 'soft AI' barriers at login.
During an outage, Gmail was down for users and coworkers across the US, UK and Brazil, including paid Google Apps accounts. Meanwhile the Apps Status Dashboard still showed green.
One user switched from Gmail to Fastmail at $90 a year and couldn't be happier not dealing with snooping and ad tracking.
